frase_gancho.texto: A painter born in Utah portrayed a wedding from Michoacán.

puente_narrativo.texto: We leave Michoacán and continue toward the Central Highlands, the land of the Otomi and the Mazahua. Look for a garment that covers the shoulders, with one point in front and another behind, embroidered with stars, birds and flowers.

guion_corto.texto: This painting is called “Purépecha Wedding.” It was made by Pablo O’Higgins, an artist born in the United States in 1904 who stayed to live in Mexico. The government granted him Mexican nationality in 1961. He was an assistant to Diego Rivera and one of the founders of the Taller de Gráfica Popular, a group of printmakers who used art to speak about ordinary people. The museum opened on September 17, 1964. For its halls, it commissioned murals from several artists, with the aim of helping visitors understand each culture. O’Higgins was given the Purépecha world. His subject is a wedding, a rite in which a community shows its clothing, its customs and its joy.

guion_largo.texto:
After the wooden house, the Viejitos (Little Old Men), the copper and the shawl, the same people appear in another way: painted on the wall, in the middle of a celebration. This is the mural “Purépecha Wedding.” In the display cases you saw objects of daily use. Here the subject is a special day in the life of a community, the day when two people get married.

It was painted by Pablo O’Higgins, and his own life is a story in itself. He was born in Salt Lake City, Utah, in 1904, and from the 1920s he lived in Mexico. He was an assistant to Diego Rivera on great works, such as the murals of the Secretaría de Educación Pública and those of Chapingo. In 1961 the Mexican government gave him nationality as an honorary distinction. He died in 1983.

He was also one of the founders of the Taller de Gráfica Popular. It was a group of artists who used printmaking to speak about workers, peasants and Indigenous peoples. O’Higgins’s work often dealt with workers and Indigenous communities. That fits a mural like this one, where the subject is a wedding and not a battle.

In 1964 the museum was about to open. It was inaugurated on September 17, and one of its goals was to teach. That is why several artists were commissioned to paint murals for the different halls. You already saw the [stained-glass window by Carlos Mérida](mna_s13_vitral_goeritz) in the Gran Nayar Hall, and you will see more. O’Higgins was commissioned for several, and this wedding is the one in the Purépecha Hall.

What can be seen in the scene? What is known is simple: it is a painting of customs around a wedding rite. The art critic Teresa del Conde wrote in 1997 about a wedding scene by O’Higgins in the ethnography halls. According to her, it is inspired by “The Dance of Life,” a painting by the Norwegian Edvard Munch about love and the ages of life. She is probably speaking of this work, although she does not name it.

A wedding is a good subject for this hall. Festive clothing, music, food and families all come together in it. Think of the shawl you saw a moment ago, which is used at baptisms and weddings. Think also of the pirekua, the Purépecha song. These are ingredients of a celebration like this one. If you find them in the mural, you will have read the scene the way you read an object in a display case.

The museum holds more works by O’Higgins. One is titled “Struggles of the Tarasco People.” Tarasco was the name the Spanish gave them, not the one they used for themselves. In 2014 that mural was restored; it had cracks from earthquakes and scratches from visitors. There is also a scene of the Sierra Tarahumara. A painter born in Utah ended up portraying, for this museum, peoples of Michoacán and Chihuahua.

Before you move on, look at the mural as if you had been invited to the party. Who might the bride and groom be? Who is accompanying whom? A wedding painted in 1964 still tells how a wedding is celebrated. That is one of the reasons the ethnography halls exist: to show the peoples of today.

texto: Look for the bride and groom among the painted figures
Notice the festive clothing: do you see a shawl like the one you just learned about?
Look at the background of the scene: what landscape surrounds the celebration?

texto.Author: Pablo O’Higgins (1904-1983)
texto.Subject: scene of customs depicting a Purépecha wedding rite

texto.pregunta: Myth: The museum’s murals are just decorations to fill the walls.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The museum commissioned them with an educational purpose, to help visitors understand each hall; “Purépecha Wedding” was painted in 1964 for the Purépecha Hall.
